snippet.title: How AMAZON Killed HMV? | The £116 Million Retail Collapse
snippet.description:
AMAZON Killed HMV. The £116M Retail Collapse | Music Store Bankruptcy Documentary
Did Amazon destroy HMV, or was it Walmart, iTunes, or management failure? Investigate the £116 million collapse of the legendary British music retail chain that dominated for 92 years. From the failed American expansion costing $9 million, to the 2013 UK bankruptcy that shocked 4,500 employees. This is the retail apocalypse story you slept through.

🔍 KEY STORY POINTS:
HMV (His Master's Voice) opened in 1921 by composer Edward Elgar. By 1990, they invaded America with 15 stores including a $1.5M/year Fifth Avenue flagship. But Walmart and Best Buy used music as loss leaders, selling CDs at $13.99 vs HMV's $18.99. HMV lost £2M annually in the US, closed all American stores by 2004, losing $9M total.

Meanwhile, Amazon launched in 1995, became the largest US music retailer by 2008. iTunes launched 2003, sold 10 billion songs by 2010. HMV failed to adapt digitally, closed 60 UK stores in 2011, sold Waterstones and Canadian operations desperately. January 15, 2013: administration with £116M debt, 4,500 jobs at risk. Second collapse in 2018.

Management admitted "serious errors" including wrong locations, failure to compete online, and ignoring digital distribution. The perfect storm: discount retailers, Amazon's rise, iTunes, streaming services, and catastrophic management decisions.

📚 LESSONS LEARNED:
• Can't compete on price without being the cheapest
• Can't compete on selection without being the best
• Can't ignore technological disruption and survive
• Loss leaders destroy specialist retail margins
• Digital adaptation requires urgency, not complacency
• American failure was a roadmap they followed to British collapse

snippet.title: The Junk Bond King: The Rise and Fall of Michael Milken (Full Documentary)
snippet.description:
Every morning in 1970, a young analyst rode a bus from New Jersey to Manhattan with a miner's headlamp strapped to his head, reading bond filings nobody else cared about. He discovered that Wall Street was pricing fear, not risk. Two decades later, he'd built a $200 billion market, made $550 million in a single year, financed CNN and the largest leveraged buyout in history, and watched federal prosecutors threaten to indict his brother unless he confessed. The prosecutors who put him away later lobbied for his pardon. He got one.

Meanwhile the content side is quietly exploding. Newsletters. Video. Creator tools. LinkedIn is slowly becoming the professional version of every other platform combined — with the most defensible data moat in the history of social media.

Everyone else sells your attention. LinkedIn sells your identity. And identity, it turns out, is worth a lot more.

LinkedIn has something no other social network on Earth possesses. Real. Verified. Professional identity. Every single user volunteers exactly who they are — their employer, their job title, their skills, their education, their entire career history. Accurately. Willingly. Because their livelihood depends on it.

That data is worth an extraordinary amount of money. Recruiters pay thousands of dollars every single month just to access it. Companies pay for job listings, sales intelligence tools, and targeted advertising aimed at professionals spending company budgets — which means the willingness to pay is almost unlimited.

Revenue hit $16 billion in 2024. Growing every single year. Profit margins expanding. And the network effect means every new professional who joins makes the platform more valuable for everyone already there.

Meanwhile the content side is quietly exploding. Newsletters. Video. Creator tools. LinkedIn is slowly becoming the professional version of every other platform combined — with the most defensible data moat in the history of social media.

Everyone else sells your attention. LinkedIn sells your identity. And identity, it turns out, is worth a lot more.

The boring professional network nobody wanted to use built the most valuable data business in social media. And Microsoft saw it coming before anyone else did.

snippet.title: The Day America SOLD Its Soul | How the Federal Reserve Was Really Born
snippet.description:
In November 1910, six men boarded a private train in Hoboken, New Jersey. They used false names. They posed as duck hunters. And they checked into a private island club on the Georgia coast, where they spent nine days drafting the law that became the Federal Reserve System. Every participant denied the meeting occurred — for twenty years. Then they confirmed it, in writing, in their own words.

In this video, we follow the documented story of the Jekyll Island meeting — who was in the room, what they built, and why the institution they created has shaped every dollar you have earned or spent since 1913.
